surprise.title: Today's Thanksgiving lands on the exact date George Washington picked for the first national one in 1789
surprise.body: On October 3, 1789, President Washington proclaimed the first Thanksgiving Day set by the new national government, and he named the date himself: "Thursday the 26th day of November next." Congress had asked for it only days after the House voted to send the First Amendment to the states, so that first one was partly a thank-you for a working Constitution. It did not stick as a yearly holiday right away. Sarah Josepha Hale, editor of Godey's Lady's Book, spent years campaigning for a national Thanksgiving and appealed directly to presidents, and Abraham Lincoln began the annual proclamations in 1863. Then in 1939, a November with five Thursdays, Franklin Roosevelt moved it a week earlier to stretch the shopping season, and people mocked the early date as "Franksgiving." Congress settled it, and on December 26, 1941, Roosevelt signed the law fixing Thanksgiving as the fourth Thursday of November. That rule is why it can only fall between November 22 and 28, and this year the calendar lines up with Washington's original choice, 237 years later. Back home it runs about 41 to 51 degrees, cloudy until midafternoon, then the sky clears around 4 PM for a clean sunset at 5:36 PM. Seventeen days until you sail on December 13.
